sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content: • **Sulh-i-kul**: The policy of 'universal peace' or absolute peace, serving as the bedrock of Akbar's religious policy, emphasizing tolerance and non-discrimination. • **Ibadat Khana**: Established in 1575 at Fatehpur Sikri, it was a 'House of Worship' for inter-faith dialogue between Sunni, Shia, Hindu, Jain, Christian, and Zoroastrian scholars. • **Mahzar (1579)**: A decree signed by leading Ulama declaring Akbar the 'Imam-i-Adil' (Just Ruler), granting him the final authority to interpret religious law in case of conflicting opinions. • **Din-i-Ilahi**: A syncretic religious path (not a formal religion) introduced in 1582, emphasizing moral conduct and loyalty to the Emperor.

The original name for Din-i-Ilahi, meaning 'Divine Monotheism', reflecting the core belief in one God and the Emperor as his shadow on earth.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content: • **Translation Bureau (Maktab Khana)**: Translation of Mahabharata (Razmnama) and Ramayana into Persian to foster cultural synthesis. • **Religious Pluralism**: Patronage to Jesuit missions (Aquaviva) and Jain scholars (Hiravijaya Suri).

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content: • **Challenges**: Resistance from orthodox Naqshbandi Sufis (e.g., Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi) and conservative Ulama. • **Solutions**: Strategic use of matrimonial alliances and administrative inclusion of Rajputs.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses 'Din-i-Ilahi' as a formal religion with a priesthood and holy book. It was a 'spiritual order' or 'discipleship' (Muridi) with no formal clergy.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Mughal Synthesis' to describe how Akbar's policies created a composite culture, bridging the gap between the ruling elite and the ruled masses.

keyTakeaways: Akbar's religious policy was a pragmatic tool for political stability and empire-building.
The Mahzar was the legal instrument that shifted power from the clergy to the state.
Social reforms were limited by the constraints of the 16th-century patriarchal society but set a precedent for state-led reform.
